construction.tiers: CustodyRecord = { v, state: 'promptless' | 'enrolling' | 'locked', seals: LockSeal[], rotation_owed }. Written at genesis on the default tier, so enabling the lock is never a schema change
construction.factors: A generated 125-bit code is mandatory and is the root; WebAuthn PRF outputs are additional seals of the same L_lock. A user-chosen passphrase is rejected: the seal sits beside the ciphertext it protects, so guessing is offline and free, and a browser origin has no rate-limiting anchor except the authenticator
construction.indirection: Factors seal a random 32-byte L_lock; L_lock opens row 3s KeyEnvelope in place of L_local. Adding, replacing or removing a factor is one 32-byte seal and moves no content and no content key
construction.kdf: K_factor = HKDF-SHA256(ikm, salt = salt[16], info = LP("done/devicelock/v1") || LP(principal_id) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(factor), L = 32)
construction.aad: LP("done/devicelock/v1") || LP(principal_id) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(decimal v) || LP(factor) || LP(id)
construction.prf_eval_input: SHA-256( LP(role label) || LP(principal_id) || LP(workspace_id) ). The separation between §13.4s four factor roles lives in this input, not in an HKDF label afterwards: four labels give four unrelated outputs, where one output and four labels gives whoever holds it all four keys
construction.length_prefix: uint16be(byteLength) || utf8 -- injective, so no field can shift another
construction.seal: LockSeal = { v: 1, factor, id, salt: 16 bytes, nonce: 12 bytes, ct: AES-256-GCM over the 32-byte L_lock, tag included }
construction.salt_note: A fresh 16-byte salt per seal means a fresh K_factor per seal and exactly one message under it, so nonce reuse is structurally unreachable rather than avoided by discipline (row 14 §4)
construction.enrollment: Seal L_lock under every factor and write state enrolling; reseal each retained generations KeyEnvelope under L_lock, staged; then one transaction swaps staged over live, deletes L_local and writes state locked. The state that must never exist -- no L_local and unresealed envelopes -- is unreachable because the delete and the swap are the same transaction
construction.rotation: Enrollment then rotates the content key forward, tracked by rotation_owed. Without it a profile copy taken before enrollment keeps opening K_g, and therefore keeps opening content written after the lock was enabled. Forward-only: history is not re-keyed, because the copy that motivated the rotation already holds it
construction.not_carried: The lock never signs, never authenticates an account, never unwraps R_priv and never becomes a recovery factor. Recovery may not open a locked slot; a lost factor re-enrolls as a device

separation_vectors.name: slot-verifier--this-slot
separation_vectors.label: done/slot-verifier-prf/v1
separation_vectors.selected_by: row 12 (review 3b) -- selected, and it uses no PRF: the verifier checks a signature rather than deriving a key, so this label is reserved and unused

separation_vectors.name: slot-verifier--other-slot
separation_vectors.label: done/slot-verifier-prf/v1
separation_vectors.selected_by: row 12 (review 3b) -- selected, and it uses no PRF: the verifier checks a signature rather than deriving a key, so this label is reserved and unused

separation_note: All eight inputs are distinct, and the generator fails if any two collide. Only the device-lock label is selected by row 13; the others are stand-ins owned by review 3bs rows, and what is asserted is that they differ rather than what they are. Row 12 has since been selected and derives nothing from a PRF output at all, so its label is reserved and unused -- §13.4s separation is satisfied structurally for that role rather than by these bytes

seal_vectors.name: code-seal
seal_vectors.why: L_lock sealed under the mandatory code. Always present: §2 of the selection makes the code the root and PRF an addition, so this is the seal every locked slot has.

inputs.ikm_note: utf8 of the canonical 25-symbol code -- the characters, not the bits packed down (row 14 §3)

seal_vectors.name: prf-seal
seal_vectors.why: The same L_lock, sealed under a PRF output. Same key, second factor: this is the property a single-factor test cannot see.

inputs.ikm_note: the 32 bytes the authenticator returns for the evaluation input above

seal_vectors.name: code-seal-other-slot
seal_vectors.why: The same code in the other workspace on one profile. Different info, different key, different ciphertext -- so a seal cannot be carried between slots.

custody_vectors.name: envelope-under-l-local
custody_vectors.why: The default tier. Row 3s vector, reproduced here so the two rows are checked against each other in one file.

custody_vectors.name: envelope-under-l-lock
custody_vectors.why: The lock tier. Same format, same AAD, same K_g, different key -- which is what "no default handle capable of opening the envelopes remains" costs in bytes.

wrapping_credential.why: L_lock protected the KeyEnvelope and left the wrapping credential beside it. On the no-PRF tier that credential is a structured-cloned non-extractable CryptoKey -- promptless, and usable from a copied profile -- so the next rotation published a reader wrap the pre-lock copy could open. It cannot be brought under the factor, because WebCrypto cannot export a non-extractable key, so the lock replaces it.

seal.note: The same LockSeal machinery as L_lock's own factor seals, with its own id bound in the AAD so the two sealed objects in a locked slot cannot be substituted for one another.

rotation_owed.derived_from: the generation-application record's step, never asserted
rotation_owed.true_while: step < 8 -- from the custody swap until the application settles
rotation_owed.why: That interval is exactly the one in which a pre-lock copy still holds K_g. Clearing it at the swap, when the envelopes move and before any rotation has landed, claims future-copy protection during precisely the window where there is none.

wrapping_credential.expected: generation g is wrapped to the pre-lock key and the successor is not; history is not re-keyed

custody_note: One KeyEnvelope, row 3s AAD byte for byte, under each tiers key. The generator reproduces row 3s published ciphertext from its published inputs and fails if either has changed, and separately asserts that L_local does not open the lock tiers envelope

must_fail.name: wrong-code
must_fail.why: A different code. The ordinary failure, and the one the copy speaks to.

must_fail.name: wrong-prf-output
must_fail.why: A different authenticator, or the right one on a different evaluation input.

must_fail.name: code-seal-as-prf
must_fail.why: A code seal opened as a prf seal. The factor kind is in both the info and the AAD, so this fails twice.

must_fail.name: prf-seal-as-code
must_fail.why: The reverse. Stated separately because an implementation can bind one direction and not the other.

must_fail.name: seal-moved-to-other-workspace
must_fail.why: A seal lifted into the other workspace on the same profile -- PRD §6.7s ordinary two-principal case, not an attack.

must_fail.name: replacement-credential-under-a-wrong-code
must_fail.why: The replacement wrapping credential is sealed with the same LockSeal machinery as L_lock itself, so a wrong code does not open it. Without this the lock would replace a promptless key with another promptless key and change nothing.

must_fail.name: replacement-credential-seal-as-a-factor-seal
must_fail.why: The credential seal presented under the code factor's own id. The seal AAD binds the id, so the two sealed objects in a locked slot -- L_lock and the wrapping credential -- cannot be substituted for one another.

must_fail.name: seal-rebound-to-other-credential
must_fail.why: A prf seal presented under another credential id, which is how a removed passkey would be made to look enrolled.

must_fail.name: downgraded-version
must_fail.why: v is in the AAD for row 1s reason: a carrier version selects the whole suite, so a renumbered seal must fail to open rather than select a weaker one.

must_fail.name: flipped-tag-bit
must_fail.why: The AEAD doing its own job.

must_fail.name: truncated-ciphertext
must_fail.why: The same, from the other end.

must_fail.name: aad-only-mislabelled-factor
must_fail.why: The correct key, with a factor the AAD disagrees about -- what an implementation that builds the AAD from a different variable than the derivation produces. Isolates the AADs binding of factor from the HKDF infos.

must_fail.name: aad-only-other-workspace
must_fail.why: The same isolation for workspace_id: correct key, AAD naming the other slot.

must_fail.name: aad-only-envelope-label
must_fail.why: The same isolation for the label, and it is the field with the least margin. This AAD and row 3's key envelope are both six length-prefixed fields with principal, workspace and v in the same three positions; the label is the whole of what separates a device-lock seal from a key envelope.
